title: Determining prenatal, early childhood and cumulative long-term lead exposure using micro-spatial deciduous dentine levels.
ehr_evidence: Mother–child pairs in this study were drawn from the longitudinal birth cohort studies in Mexico City that comprise the Early Life Exposures in MExico and NeuroToxicology (ELEMENT) project.
summary: In a prospective mother-child cohort (ELEMENT, Mexico City) of 85 subjects, micro-spatial deciduous dentine lead levels were validated against maternal blood/bone, umbilical cord blood, and serial childhood blood lead to assess exposure timing over prenatal, early childhood, and cumulative long-term periods.
key_findings: Dentine Pb at the neonatal line was significantly associated with cord blood Pb (Spearman r = 0.69; n = 27; p<0.0001).
Prenatal dentine Pb was significantly associated with maternal patella Pb (Spearman r = 0.48; n = 59; p<0.0001), a stronger association than with tibia Pb (Spearman r = 0.35; n = 41; p<0.03).
Dentine Pb formed at 3 months was significantly associated with child blood Pb measured concurrently (Spearman r = 0.64; n = 55; p<0.0001), with progressively weaker associations at older ages.
Second trimester maternal blood Pb was associated with prenatal dentine Pb (Spearman r = 0.60; n = 36; p<0.0001) and third trimester (Spearman r = 0.64; n = 44; p<0.0001).
Mean Pb in secondary dentine correlated positively with cumulative blood lead index (Spearman r = 0.38; n = 75; p<0.0007).
Birth dentine Pb was not significantly associated with child blood Pb sampled after 2 years of age.
Secondary dentine Pb was not significantly associated with maternal bone or maternal blood during pregnancy (all p>0.05).
captured_features: Micro-spatial dentine Pb (208Pb:43Ca) by LA-ICP-MS in primary and secondary dentine
Maternal venous blood Pb by trimester
Maternal bone Pb (tibia, patella) by K-XRF
Child blood Pb at 3, 6, 18, 30 months and later ages
Tooth type and age at shedding
population: 85 mother-child pairs from the ELEMENT cohort in Mexico City; children followed from birth to 6 years with blood Pb up to 7-11 years; deciduous teeth collected at 7-15 years
limitations: Incomplete set of biomarkers on all 85 participants due to incomplete follow-up and sample collection.
Only one tooth per participant, preventing exploration of tooth-type influence on dentine Pb.
